messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
For the implication from completeness to the property, we may assume M is complete and we take (F_n) to be nested nonempty closed sets with diam F_n→0.
How does one extract a Cauchy sequence from this data?
We choose x_n∈F_n, and since x_m∈F_n whenever m≥n, we have d(x_m,x_n)≤diam F_n, and diam F_n→0, so (x_n) is Cauchy.
Completeness yields x_n→x, and closedness of F_n forces x∈F_n for every n because all later x_m lie in F_n.
Thus the intersection is nonempty, which is exactly the required implication.
Conversely, how does one turn a Cauchy sequence into nested closed sets of vanishing diameter?
Given a Cauchy sequence (y_n), we define F_n=\overline{\{y_m:m\ge n\}}, and we observe, because (y_n) is Cauchy, that these sets are nonempty, closed, nested, and have diameters tending to zero.
The stated property gives x∈∩_n F_n, and since y_n∈F_n, d(x,y_n)≤diam F_n, and diam F_n→0, so y_n→x and M is complete.
Does this establish the equivalence?
